newsitem.title: USA: SF Fed's Parry sees some pickup in wages, salaries.
newsitem.headline: SF Fed's Parry sees some pickup in wages, salaries.

text.p: U.S. compensation costs appear to have accelerated, although probably mildly, the head of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco said Tuesday.

"Our statistics on basic compensation -- that is wages and salaries -- suggest that there may be some pickup that is occurring, but it isn't a very sharp one," San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry said.
Parry was responding to a question at an event sponsored by the Financial Women's Association and the Financial Institutions Marketing Association.
Referring to the 3.3 percent reading on the overall Consumer Price Index in 1996, Parry said, "I think we can do better than that."

He added, "That doesn't mean we can do it in 1997, but I think in terms of a longer-term objective, we probably would increase our confidence in having a stable, acceptable long-run rate of growth if the inflation were even a bit lower."
On the subject of whether slow growth in other industrial economies could be a factor in restraining inflation, Parry expressed skepticism.

"The effect of the slack in the world economy is a little more complicated than you might think," he said, noting that if U.S. demand picks up strongly in comparison to other countries, any effects on inflation might be offset by exchange-rate developments.
Speaking to reporters following his remarks, Parry predicted a slightly higher rate of underlying U.S. inflation this year compared to last year.
In 1996, the core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose by 2.6 percent, the smallest rise since an identical increase in 1994.
"If the economy grows as I expect it to grow, it's possible we could see some slight upward pressure on the core rate of inflation," he said.

"If I had to guess in terms of (the) core rate of inflation, it would pick up," Parry said, adding the 1997 rate would likely be higher by "a couple of tenths" of a percentage point than the 1996 rate.

Asked about the implications of developments with the U.S. dollar on the inflation picture, Parry responded, "One of the things that works in the direction of maybe taking a little bit of pressure off of our resources is a higher value of dollar."
"As a result, it's a factor that maybe keeps a little bit of downward pressure on inflation as well," he said.
